article.title: CCTV Rules in Dubai
article.author: Sejal Desai
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Security cameras are standard in Dubai shops, warehouses and offices, yet many employers overlook the legal side. A camera that records staff is collecting personal data, and that changes how it must be planned, explained and managed. This article covers the main rules on employee monitoring in the UAE, from camera placement to footage storage. The Legal Framework Behind Workplace Cameras Two sets of rules matter. Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on the Protection of Personal Data treats identifiable images of people as personal data, so recorded footage falls within its scope. The UAE Data Office is named as the federal regulator. Businesses in the DIFC and ADGM follow their own data protection regimes instead. The second layer is local. In Dubai, Law No. 12 of 2016 regulates the security industry and created the Security Industry Regulatory Agency (SIRA), which licenses and supervises security service providers, including firms that install surveillance systems. Employers should check the current status of the federal law's executive regulations before finalising any policy. For a practical summary of how these layers fit together, this guide to CCTV rules in Dubai is a useful reference. Where Cameras Can and Cannot Go Placement should follow a genuine risk. Entrances, reception desks, cash points, safes, stockrooms and server rooms are usually easy to justify for security, safety or loss prevention. Wide shots of shared work areas can be reasonable if the purpose is disclosed to staff. Some spaces are off limits. Toilets, changing rooms, prayer rooms and private rest areas should never be filmed. A gym, for instance, may cover its reception and training floor but not its locker rooms. A camera trained on one employee's desk, or one that captures neighbouring units or public areas without good reason, is likely to be seen as excessive. Audio deserves special caution. Take legal advice before recording conversations. Clearly notified call recording in a defined customer service role is easier to defend than general office audio. Telling Staff and Writing a Policy Transparency is central. Put clear signs at entrances and in monitored zones stating that CCTV is in operation, why it is used and who to contact with questions. Repeat the same information in employment contracts or the staff handbook. A written monitoring policy should explain the purpose of each camera, the areas covered, and any monitoring of email, company devices or work systems. Ask each employee to acknowledge it in writing, and keep the policy consistent with UAE labour rules and your internal grievance process. Company accounts and devices are easier to monitor lawfully than personal ones. If personal devices are involved, set firm limits and obtain consent. Covert monitoring should be avoided unless legal advice supports it. Installing and Reviewing the System Start by mapping each camera to a specific risk. A logistics firm might justify two cameras at a loading bay after past theft. Then use a SIRA-licensed provider rather than fitting consumer cameras yourself, and keep installation records and a camera map. Give staff a fair way to raise objections. If an employee feels a camera is too close to their workstation, the complaint should go through the normal HR procedure and be reviewed on its merits. Review the setup periodically. Storing and Sharing Footage Securely Footage should sit in a secure system with access limited to named managers. Log every viewing and export, and set a fixed retention period that is applied consistently. Some activities carry minimum retention requirements, so confirm the rule for your sector with the relevant authority. Connected cameras also need protection: change default passwords, keep firmware updated, encrypt stored footage and place cameras on a network separate from office systems. When someone requests footage, confirm who they are and why they need it. Share it only for a lawful reason, such as a police request, record each disclosure and blur third parties where appropriate. Delete recordings once they are no longer needed. Conclusion Compliant workplace monitoring in Dubai rests on four principles: a clear purpose, proportionate coverage, open communication with staff and secure handling of footage. Documenting each decision makes recordings easier to rely on in a dispute. These principles apply across the emirate's business zones, including free zone companies such as those licensed in Meydan Free Zone , which should also confirm any premises rules with their landlord before installing cameras.
